intro: It is the tallest clock tower on Earth, with four faces 43 meters across and a golden crescent 23 meters wide, built on ground where an Ottoman fortress stood for two centuries. This is how Mecca got its own time.
page_title: Abraj Al Bait: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The Abraj Al Bait, the Towers of the House, is a seven-tower complex built by the Saudi Binladin Group to designs by Dar Al-Handasah, directly across from the Masjid al-Haram. Construction ran from 2004 to 2012 at a reported cost of about 15 billion dollars. The central Makkah Royal Clock Tower rises 601 meters, with 76 stories of hotel rooms, a prayer hall for about 4,000 worshippers, a lunar observation center, and an Islamic museum. The six flanking towers, named Hajar, Zamzam, Maqam, Qibla, Safa and Marwa, hold thousands more hotel rooms for the millions who come for Hajj and Umrah each year.
sections.heading: A tower for the pilgrims

sections.body: The clock was designed by the German firm PERROT and began trial operation in Ramadan 2010. Its four faces are 43 meters in diameter, the largest clock faces ever built, faced with 98 million pieces of glass mosaic and lit by about 2 million LEDs. The minute hand alone is 22 meters long, the hour hand 17 meters, both in carbon fiber. At the call to prayer, 21,000 green and white LEDs set the whole clock ablaze, visible from 30 kilometers away. Five atomic clocks keep it tied to UTC, and the project openly proposed its time as Mecca Time, a rival reference to Greenwich.
sections.heading: The largest clock in the world

sections.body: The towers stand on the Bulbul hill, where the Ottoman Ajyad Fortress had watched over Mecca since the 18th century. In 2002 the fortress was demolished to clear the site, and the demolition was condemned around the world: heritage bodies called it the destruction of one of the last Ottoman landmarks in Arabia, and Turkish officials protested formally. The Saudi authorities argued the fortress stood in the way of facilities the pilgrims needed. The argument over the fortress became the defining controversy of the project: a debate about whether serving the pilgrims of today justified erasing the Mecca of the past.
sections.heading: The fortress that was in the way

sections.body: Above the clock, a 93-meter needle carries the golden crescent: 23 meters across, the largest crescent ever built, the symbol of Islam set at 601 meters. Below it sits the lunar observation deck, where astronomers sight the new moon that opens each Islamic month. The whole assembly of clock, needle and crescent is 251 meters tall by itself, taller than most skyscrapers. At night the tower is a beacon: the calligraphy band glows, the crescent shines, and the time it shows is meant to be the time of the Muslim world.
sections.heading: The crescent on top

sections.body:
The tower has never needed a film role; it has the Hajj. Every year, when two million pilgrims circle the Kaaba, the clock tower looms in the background of the news footage beamed around the world, and it has become the visual shorthand for the modern, vertical Mecca in a way no fiction could arrange.

Its loudest cultural moment was the fight over what it replaced. The 2002 demolition of the Ajyad Fortress drew condemnation from heritage organizations and the Turkish government, and the coverage, from the BBC to architectural journals, framed the tower as the symbol of a larger argument about development in the holy cities. The tower is routinely cited in that debate, the prime exhibit whenever Mecca's transformation is discussed.

The clock itself entered the cultural conversation as a statement of intent. The proposal of Mecca Time, kept by five atomic clocks and broadcast from the largest faces on Earth, was reported worldwide as a direct challenge to Greenwich Mean Time. Whether or not the world sets its watches by it, the tower succeeded in its real aim: nobody photographs Mecca now without it.
sections.heading: In the cultural conversation

timeline.text: The Ottoman Ajyad Fortress is demolished to clear the site, drawing international condemnation.
Construction of the Abraj Al Bait complex begins.
The clock begins trial operation during Ramadan.
The Makkah Royal Clock Tower is completed at 601 meters, the tallest clock tower in the world.
